title: Two people, one plan
teaches: When marriage raises or lowers a couple's tax, how unmarried partners are treated for tax and health credits, and the higher tax a survivor pays on the same savings

parts.title: A couple is not two singles

blocks.text: Most of this course used a married couple filing jointly. The joint return doubles most of the single thresholds, so a couple with similar incomes pays about what two single people would. But not every line is doubled, and the ones that aren't matter most to the households this course has in mind: retirees with large pre-tax accounts, early retirees on the marketplace, and the partner left behind.

**Bonuses.** When one partner earns most of the income, marriage lowers the tax. The joint brackets up to 35 percent are exactly twice the single ones, so the high earner's income is taxed as if it were split evenly between the two of them. A single earner on $200,000 who marries a partner with no income cuts their federal tax by more than a quarter, from about $36,700 to $26,300.

**Penalties.** Several lines are not doubled. The 37 percent bracket starts at $768,700 for a couple in 2026, well below twice the single threshold of $640,600. The 3.8 percent tax on investment income starts at $250,000 for a couple against $200,000 for each single person. For those who itemise, state and local taxes paid can be deducted only up to a cap, $40,400 for a married couple, the same as for one single person, so two itemising singles who marry lose half their allowance. And the tax on Social Security starts at $32,000 of provisional income (other income plus half the benefits, lesson 12) for a couple against $25,000 each for two singles, a gap that hasn't been adjusted since 1984.

For most retired couples, penalties and bonuses roughly cancel. Where they don't, the difference is rarely a reason to marry or not, but it is a reason to know whether a household gains or loses by it.

The largest difference for early retirees is the ACA. An unmarried couple without children in common are two households of one, each with its own poverty line and its own cliff. Two single people can each have MAGI up to $62,600 in 2026 before losing the credit, $125,200 together, against $84,600 for a married couple. A pair of partners planning large Roth conversions before 65 has nearly half as much again in room unmarried as married.

Other things favour marriage: Social Security's spousal and survivor benefits, the unlimited marital deduction, which lets anything left to a spouse pass free of estate tax, the right to roll over a spouse's IRA, and Washington's community property rules, which also apply to registered domestic partners under state law.[^rdp] Couples who stay unmarried for the ACA lose the federal ones, and unless they register as domestic partners, the state ones too. They need wills and beneficiary forms that do by choice what marriage does by default.

When one spouse dies, the other files jointly for that year and then, unless they have a dependent child, as a single person. Their income usually falls only a little: the IRAs are still there and must still be drawn, and of the two Social Security benefits the larger continues. But the brackets and the standard deduction halve, so income that was taxed at 12 percent for the couple can reach 22 or 24 percent for one person.

blocks.caption: Federal tax for a couple over 65 and for the survivor the year after a death, with the same IRA withdrawals and the smaller Social Security benefit gone.

blocks.text: The figure starts at the example here. A couple taking $100,000 from IRAs with benefits of $40,000 and $25,000 pays about $13,300 in federal tax. The survivor, with $25,000 less coming in, pays about $19,800. Medicare's surcharges, too, start at $109,000 of MAGI for a single person, half the couple's line. The required withdrawals from accounts that were sized for two now fall on one return.

This is a strong argument for the conversions of lesson 10 while both are alive. Converting at the couple's 12 or 22 percent spares the survivor withdrawals at 24 or 32, often for many years, since one spouse often outlives the other by a decade or more.[^gap] The higher earner delaying Social Security to 70 (lesson 13) helps too, since the larger benefit is the one the survivor keeps.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Marriage lowers the tax when incomes are unequal, and raises it at the top bracket, the investment income tax and the Social Security thresholds.
Unmarried partners each get their own ACA cliff: $125,200 of combined MAGI against $84,600 for a married couple.
Staying unmarried gives up survivor benefits, the marital deduction and spousal rollovers.
The survivor files single on nearly the same income, and pays more tax and Medicare surcharge for it.
Roth conversions while both are alive protect the survivor.

blocks.caption: Four questions on couples
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A high earner marries someone with no income. What usually happens to their federal tax?
choices: It falls, because the joint brackets are twice as wide
It rises, because of the marriage penalty
items.why: With one income, the doubled brackets work entirely in the couple's favour.

items.ask: An unmarried couple of 60 with no children together want to keep their ACA credits. What is their combined MAGI limit in 2026?
items.why: Each is a household of one with a cliff at $62,600.

items.ask: Why does a widow often pay more tax than the couple did?
choices: She files single with nearly the same IRA withdrawals
Survivor benefits are taxed at a higher rate
Her IRA withdrawals are taxed at a special survivor rate
items.why: Income falls a little but the brackets and the standard deduction halve.

items.ask: Which plan best protects a survivor from high brackets?
choices: Roth conversions while both spouses are alive
Delaying all IRA withdrawals until required
Claiming the larger Social Security benefit early
items.why: Converting at the couple's lower rates shrinks the pre-tax balance the survivor would draw at single rates.

summary: **Joint brackets are double the single ones, mostly.** Unequal incomes gain from marriage.
**Some lines aren't doubled.** The top bracket, the investment income tax, the SALT cap and the Social Security thresholds.
**Unmarried partners get two ACA cliffs.** $125,200 of room together against $84,600 married.
**Marriage brings protections.** Survivor benefits, the marital deduction and spousal rollovers.
**The survivor's brackets halve.** Nearly the same income is taxed as a single person's.
**Convert while both are alive.** It spares the survivor years of higher rates.

rdp.title: Domestic partners
rdp.text: Washington's registered domestic partnerships, now mostly for couples where one partner is 62 or older, carry the state rights of marriage, including community property. Federal tax doesn't recognise them: partners file as single people, though the IRS requires them to split community income between their returns.

gap.title: How long the survivor lives
gap.text: For a man and a woman both 65, the chance that one of them reaches 90 is about one in two, and the survivor's years alone average around ten. Plans that stop at the first death understate the years at single rates.
